subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Exoplanet Weather
description: A micro-lesson that makes Exoplanet Weather usable.

hook.text: Exoplanet weather makes Earth's worst storms look gentle. Some worlds have winds over 8,000 km/h and molten glass rain.

buildup.text: HD 189733b is a hot Jupiter with silicate clouds. The rain is literally molten glass blown sideways by hypersonic winds.

discovery.text: Phase curve observations track brightness changes as the planet rotates, mapping temperature differences across its surface.

twist.text: Some hot Jupiters have day-side temperatures of 4,600°C—hotter than many stars. Iron and titanium vaporize there.

climax.text: WASP-76b may have iron rain: iron vaporizes on the scorching day side and condenses into rain on the cooler night side.

punchline.text: Glass rain, iron rain, hypersonic winds. Alien weather at its most extreme.

quiz.question: What makes the weather on WASP-76b so extreme?
options: Iron vaporizes on the day side and rains down as liquid on the cooler night side
It has permanent hurricanes larger than the planet Jupiter
Its entire atmosphere freezes and thaws every orbit

details.summary: Exoplanet weather is far more extreme than anything on Earth. Observations have revealed raining molten iron on WASP-76b, 8,000 km/h winds on HD 189733b, and silicate particle clouds on hot gas giants.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding exoplanet weather reveals atmospheric dynamics, energy transport, and chemistry on worlds vastly different from Earth — broadening our understanding of how planetary atmospheres work.
takeaways: Extreme conditions include molten iron rain and supersonic winds
JWST maps temperature and chemistry across exoplanet surfaces
Weather patterns reveal atmospheric dynamics and composition

faq.question: How do we know it rains iron on WASP-76b?
faq.answer: Transmission spectroscopy revealed iron vapor in the atmosphere of the scorching day side (2,400°C) but not on the cooler night side. The iron condenses as it circulates to the night side and falls as liquid iron rain.

faq.question: Can we map weather patterns on exoplanets?
faq.answer: Yes, using phase curves — measuring brightness changes as the planet rotates. Hot spots offset from the sub-stellar point reveal wind patterns.
